title: Reading drawings and schematics
where: the Engineering science shelf's Engineering science folder
folderRuns: Mechanics and materials, Heat and fluids, then Reading drawings and schematics
blurb: How to read any system diagram: electrical schematics, hydraulic and pneumatic circuits, piping diagrams and engineering drawings.
from: any Brilliant course still reachable on brilliant.org that teaches reading diagrams (none is expected), and failing that the public benchmark of a Level 3 engineering unit on engineering drawing and on fluid power circuits (Pearson BTEC National Engineering units on engineering drawing or computer aided drawing, on hydraulic and pneumatic systems, and on electrical and electronic principles where circuit diagrams are read)
others: the standards as titled descriptions only (ISO 1219-1 and 1219-2 fluid power symbols and circuit diagrams, IEC 60617 graphical symbols for diagrams, IEC 61082 preparation of electrotechnical documents, IEC 81346 reference designations, ISO 10628 and ISO 14617 for process and piping diagrams, ISA 5.1 instrument tags, BS 8888 and ISO 128 for technical drawings, first-angle and third-angle projection symbols), and for the symbols themselves the public material that reproduces them: fluid power makers' training guides and symbol charts (Bosch Rexroth, Parker, Festo Didactic, Eaton/Vickers industrial hydraulics material, SMC), the public US Navy NEETS and fluid power training manuals where they are openly published (as general training text, never as how any navy does things), All About Circuits (ladder and schematic diagrams), Engineering ToolBox P&ID symbol pages, HSE guidance that shows isolation and schematic conventions, university open courseware on engineering drawing, and OpenStax or LibreTexts where a physical idea needs it
syllabi: What a marine or naval engineering technician on the electrical path must be able to read: the public apprenticeship standards on the Institute for Apprenticeships site for a Marine engineer, Naval engineering technician (or nearest), Engineering technician and Maintenance and operations engineering technician, with their lines on reading and interpreting engineering drawings, circuit diagrams, schematics and system diagrams; the STCW Code Tables A-III/1 and A-III/6 lines on interpreting electrical and electronic diagrams and on piping, hydraulic and pneumatic diagrams; and the Pearson BTEC Level 3 unit lines on engineering drawing and on fluid power circuit diagrams. Exact lines. Dan has no syllabi for his Navy courses ahead: plan against these and say where a choice is a guess
scope: Dan asked (13 Nov): "A schematics and drawings interpretation course would actually be really useful", and of the four kinds below, "they all matter and not in any order". He has to learn system diagrams for his submarine qualification; this course never uses, shows or describes those diagrams or any Navy drawing (they are not public), and never claims how the Navy or any boat draws or lays out anything. It teaches the public conventions so that any diagram in those styles can be read: what each symbol means, what the lines mean, what state the diagram shows, and how to trace a path through it. He is a qualified electrician (BS 7671 design, inspection and testing): he reads installation circuit diagrams and wiring diagrams already, so the electrical lessons start above that, at single-line distribution diagrams and control schematics with cross-references. About nine lessons in about this order (the brief may merge or split, and may reorder so the four kinds are balanced): (1) How any diagram talks: a diagram shows function, not shape or position; symbols, lines and junctions; the legend and the title block; the state a diagram is drawn in (de-energised, unpressurised, valves in their normal position); reference designations and tags; reading from source to load. (2) Single-line diagrams: generators, busbars, breakers, isolators, transformers, converters and loads as one line; reading a distribution from each source to each load; what opens to isolate a load, and what a bus-tie does. (3) Control schematics: coils and their contacts drawn apart and linked by a reference; normally open and normally closed contacts drawn de-energised; rungs and cross-references; schematic against wiring diagram against block diagram; tracing a start and stop circuit with an interlock and saying what each contact is doing now. (4) Fluid power symbols: the reservoir, pump, motor, cylinder, filter, cooler, accumulator and gauge; working, pilot and drain lines; lines crossing and joining; why a symbol shows what a part does, not how it is built. (5) Valves in fluid power: a directional valve as boxes, one per position, with its ports and its ways (4/3, 5/2, 3/2); how it is operated and returned (lever, solenoid, pilot, spring); centre conditions; pressure relief and reducing valves, check valves and flow controls. (6) Tracing a hydraulic circuit: for each valve position, follow the oil from the pump to the actuator and back to the tank, say what moves and which way, what holds a load, what limits pressure and speed; then the same reading for a pneumatic circuit and what differs (air exhausts, service unit, compressibility). (7) Piping and system diagrams: pipes, valve types (gate, globe, ball, butterfly, non-return, relief, three-way), pumps, tanks, strainers and heat exchangers; instrument bubbles and tag letters in outline; line types; tracing a flow path, finding what isolates a part, and what a cross-connection allows. (8) Engineering drawings: views of one object (first-angle projection, with third-angle named), hidden and centre lines, sections and hatching, dimensions and tolerances, scale, the title block and revisions. (9) Reading one you have never seen: a method that works on any diagram (find the legend, the sources and the sinks, the normal state, then trace one path at a time), then mixed puzzles across all four kinds, including what-if questions (this valve shut, this contact open, this breaker tripped: what stops, and what still runs). Each lesson opens with a puzzle he can feel his way through, then the rule, then puzzles he answers by tapping the diagram or typing. Interactives where he traces a path by tapping parts in order, switches a valve or a contact and watches what moves or lights, matches a symbol to what it does, and picks the view that matches an object. Every diagram is the course's own drawing of a generic system (a workshop press, a cooling water loop, a compressed air system, a fuel transfer system, a pump's starter, a small generator-fed switchboard), drawn to the public symbol conventions; never a copy of any real installation's drawing. Symbols must be drawn accurately to the standard conventions, and where two conventions are in common use (IEC against ANSI electrical symbols, ISO against older fluid power symbols, first against third angle) teach the ISO, IEC and BS form and show the other as one to recognise. No reactor, weapons or propulsion plant content
